milestones.title: regret, greedy and epsilon-greedy
milestones.task: Write pseudo_regret(probs, counts), greedy(counts, totals, t, rng), epsilon_greedy(counts, totals, t, rng, eps=0.1) and mean_regret(select, probs, steps, seeds). Untried arms are pulled first, lowest index first; ties go to the lowest index.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand values first (regret 3.0 for the pulls above; greedy picks arm 1 from averages 0.2, 0.8, 0.4; an untried arm always goes first), then statistics: with ε = 0.3 about 20% of the pulls (ε times 2/3 for three arms) must land off the best arm, over thousands of seeded draws. Then the experiment: over 100 seeds on the 0.30, 0.45, 0.50 bandit, greedy loses well over 100 in 2,000 pulls and epsilon-greedy under 80, and on an easy 0.2, 0.5, 0.8 bandit epsilon-greedy's regret must keep growing in a straight line from 500 to 4,000 pulls.
hints: pseudo_regret is one line: sum(n * (best - p) for n, p in zip(counts, probs)).

greedy: scan for the first counts[i] == 0 and return it. Otherwise compute totals[i] / counts[i] for each arm and take the arg-max. max(range(k), key=...) returns the first maximiser, which gives you the lowest-index tie-break for free if the key is only the average.

epsilon_greedy: use exactly one rng.random() to decide whether to explore, and rng.randrange(len(counts)) only when exploring. An exploring pull may land on the best arm, which is why the check expects ε × 2/3, not ε.
mean_regret: run_bandit(select, probs, steps, seed) returns (counts, totals); feed the counts to pseudo_regret and average over the seeds.
milestones.solution:
def pseudo_regret(probs, counts):
    """R = sum_i counts[i] * (mu_star - mu_i): what the pulls cost against always playing the best arm."""
    best = max(probs)
    return sum(n * (best - p) for n, p in zip(counts, probs))

def greedy(counts, totals, t, rng):
    """Try every arm once (lowest index first), then always pull the arm with the best average.
    Ties go to the lowest index."""
    for i, n in enumerate(counts):
        if n == 0:
            return i
    avg = [s / n for n, s in zip(counts, totals)]
    return max(range(len(avg)), key=lambda i: (avg[i], -i))

def epsilon_greedy(counts, totals, t, rng, eps=0.1):
    """With probability eps pull a uniformly random arm; otherwise act greedily (untried arms first)."""
    if rng.random() < eps:
        return rng.randrange(len(counts))
    return greedy(counts, totals, t, rng)

def mean_regret(select, probs, steps, seeds):
    """Average pseudo-regret of a policy over the given seeds."""
    total = 0.0
    for seed in seeds:
        counts, _ = run_bandit(select, probs, steps, seed)
        total += pseudo_regret(probs, counts)
    return total / len(seeds)
milestones.explain:
A multi-armed bandit is a row of slot machines. Each arm pays 1 with a fixed probability you cannot see, and 0 otherwise. You have a budget of pulls and want as much reward as possible. Nothing changes between pulls, so there is no tree: only the dilemma of whether to pull the arm that looks best so far or an arm you know little about. The code keeps two lists, counts[i] (pulls of arm i) and totals[i] (reward collected from it), and every policy is a function of those lists:

def policy(counts, totals, t, rng):    # returns the index of the arm to pull; t is the 1-based number of this pull

To compare policies we need one number. Regret is the reward you gave up compared with an all-knowing player who pulled the best arm every time. In a simulation we know the true win rates, so we can compute the expected loss exactly. With best mean μ*, true means μi and pull counts ni:

R = ∑i ni · (μ* − μi)

(Strictly this is pseudo-regret: it uses the arms' means, not the noisy rewards actually received, which removes luck from the comparison.) On the bandit with win rates 0.30, 0.45 and 0.50, pulling the 0.45 arm costs 0.05 per pull and the 0.30 arm costs 0.20, so 10, 20 and 70 pulls of the three arms have regret 10 × 0.20 + 20 × 0.05 + 0 = 3.0.

Two policies to write. Greedy tries every arm once, lowest index first, then always pulls the arm with the best average so far. Its weakness is lock-in: if the best arm happens to lose on its first pulls, its average is low, greedy never goes back, and regret grows in proportion to the number of pulls. Epsilon-greedy repairs this by exploring with probability ε: draw one random number, and if it is below ε pull a uniformly random arm, otherwise act greedily. It never gets locked in. But it keeps exploring for ever, so even after it has found the best arm a fraction of its pulls are wasted, and its regret still grows in a straight line, with a small slope. You will measure that slope.

The last function, mean_regret, wraps the given run_bandit in a loop over seeds. It is small, but every later bandit milestone uses it, and it is where you learn that one run proves nothing: a single run of any of these policies is dominated by luck.

Common misconception

"Greedy is fine if the arms are different enough." The danger is not that greedy cannot tell arms apart, but that it stops looking. After a few unlucky early pulls it never gathers the evidence that would correct the mistake. The check runs greedy over 100 seeds on a bandit with a 0.05 gap and makes you see how often that happens: it asserts that greedy's mean regret exceeds 100 in 2,000 pulls, and prints it.
milestones.card:
A bandit is a row of slot machines, called arms. Each arm pays 1 with a hidden probability and 0 otherwise, and you get a fixed number of pulls. Every pull is a choice between exploiting (the arm that looks best so far) and exploring (an arm you know little about). Regret is what that choice costs: the reward you gave up compared with pulling the best arm every time.

pseudo_regret(probs, counts) uses the true win rates probs, which a real player never sees: each arm costs its pull count times how far its rate falls below the best rate. greedy sees only counts (pulls per arm) and totals (reward per arm), so an untried arm has no average and goes first. epsilon_greedy draws one number from rng: below eps it pulls a uniformly random arm (the greedy one included), otherwise it defers to greedy. mean_regret runs the given run_bandit for each seed and averages the regret of the counts it returns.

win rates 0.30, 0.45, 0.50; pulls 10, 20, 70
regret = 10*0.20 + 20*0.05 + 70*0 = 3.0

milestones.title: UCB1, optimism under uncertainty
milestones.task: Write ucb_scores(counts, totals, t, c) (the list of bounds, with math.inf for untried arms) and ucb1(counts, totals, t, rng, c=1.0) (the arm with the highest bound; ties to the lowest index).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand values (the three bounds above, 1.221, 1.520 and 1.442 at c = 1), infinite bounds for untried arms even at c = 0, c = 0 equal to greedy, and an arm that is left alone while t grows until its bound overtakes the leader's. Then the experiment: on the chapter bandit UCB1 with c = 0.5 must beat both the textbook c = 1.41 and an over-greedy c = 0.2, and on an easy bandit its regret may grow by less than 2.5 times between 500 and 4,000 pulls (a straight line would be 8 times).
hints: Compute the bound arm by arm in a loop; for n == 0 append math.inf instead of evaluating the formula.
math.sqrt(math.log(t) / n). Multiply the bonus by c, not the average.
ucb1 should call ucb_scores rather than repeat the formula. For the tie-break use max(range(len(s)), key=lambda i: (s[i], -i)): the pair compares the score first, then prefers the smaller index.
If the experiment fails but the hand values pass, print the regret of partial(ucb1, c=...) for a few values of c and see where the minimum is.
milestones.solution:
def ucb_scores(counts, totals, t, c):
    """UCB_i = mean_i + c * sqrt(ln t / n_i) for every arm. An untried arm has an infinite bound."""
    out = []
    for n, s in zip(counts, totals):
        if n == 0:
            out.append(math.inf)
        else:
            out.append(s / n + c * math.sqrt(math.log(t) / n))
    return out

def ucb1(counts, totals, t, rng, c=1.0):
    """Pull the arm with the highest upper confidence bound (ties to the lowest index)."""
    scores = ucb_scores(counts, totals, t, c)
    return max(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: (scores[i], -i))
milestones.explain:
Epsilon-greedy explores blindly: it is as likely to re-test an arm it has pulled a thousand times as one it has pulled twice. UCB1 (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer, 2002) explores where it is ignorant. It scores each arm with an upper confidence bound, a number that the arm's true mean is unlikely to exceed, and pulls the arm with the highest bound:

UCBi = x̄i + c √( ln t / ni )

Here x̄i is the arm's average reward, ni its pulls, t the number of the pull being chosen and c an exploration constant. The second term is the bonus. It is large when ni is small and shrinks as the arm is tried. The ln t on top grows very slowly, so an arm that is left alone for a long time creeps back up the ranking until it gets another look. The principle is called optimism in the face of uncertainty: act as if each arm is as good as it plausibly could be, and let the evidence correct you.

A worked example makes the trade-off concrete. Three arms have been pulled 4, 2 and 1 times with totals 2, 1 and 0, so their averages are 0.5, 0.5 and 0.0. It is pull t = 8, and ln 8 = 2.08. The least-tried arm C has the worst average but the biggest bonus. Which arm wins depends on c:

import math
from solution import *

counts, totals, t = [4, 2, 1], [2.0, 1.0, 0.0], 8
for c in (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
    scores = ucb_scores(counts, totals, t, c)
    pick = ucb1(counts, totals, t, None, c)
    print(f"c={c:<3}  scores " + "  ".join(f"{s:.3f}" for s in scores) + f"   -> pull arm {'ABC'[pick]}")
$ python3 exp_ucb.py
c=0.0  scores 0.500  0.500  0.000   -> pull arm A
c=0.5  scores 0.861  1.010  0.721   -> pull arm B
c=1.0  scores 1.221  1.520  1.442   -> pull arm B
c=2.0  scores 1.942  2.539  2.884   -> pull arm C

With c = 0 the bonus vanishes and UCB1 is greedy (it pulls A, the first of the tied leaders). At c = 0.5 and 1 the moderately-tried arm B wins, since its bonus is bigger than A's and its average is better than C's. At c = 2 the bonus dominates and the never-successful arm C is pulled. The Hoeffding inequality derivation in the chapter gives c = √2 ≈ 1.41 as the safe worst-case value; as the chapter showed, on a real problem it is often too cautious.

Two implementation details matter. An arm with zero pulls would divide by zero; give it an infinite bound so it is tried first (which also means math.log(t) is always defined when the formula is used, since at least K pulls have happened). And break ties towards the lowest index, so the check is repeatable.
milestones.card:
A policy that explores at random is as likely to re-test an arm pulled a thousand times as one pulled twice. UCB1 (upper confidence bound) explores where it is ignorant: it gives every arm an optimistic score, a guess at the highest win rate the arm plausibly has, and pulls the arm with the best score. As an arm is tried, its doubt shrinks and its average takes over.

ucb_scores(counts, totals, t, c) returns one score per arm: its average reward plus a bonus c * sqrt(ln t / n). Here n is the arm's pulls, ln is math.log, t is the number of the pull being chosen (the first is 1) and c sets how adventurous to be. An arm with no pulls would divide by zero, so give it math.inf. ucb1 calls ucb_scores and returns the index of the largest score, the lowest index on a tie.

pulls 4, 2, 1; rewards 2, 1, 0; t = 8; c = 1
scores 1.221, 1.520, 1.442 -> pull arm 1

Read more: A7 chapter 1, exploration versus exploitation.

milestones.title: Thompson sampling
milestones.task: Write thompson(counts, totals, t, rng): for each arm, in index order, one rng.betavariate(1 + wins, 1 + losses) where wins is totals[i] and losses is counts[i] - totals[i]; return the arm with the largest draw (earliest on a tie).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. A scripted generator checks the Beta parameters and the call order by hand ((8, 4), (2, 4), (4, 4) for 7/10, 1/4 and 3/6); then seeded statistics: 900 wins of 1,000 against 100 of 1,000 is always followed, three untried arms are picked about equally, and the wider belief of a 1 in 2 arm wins a sizeable minority of draws against a 5 in 10 arm. Finally the experiment: on the chapter bandit Thompson sampling must beat greedy, epsilon-greedy and the textbook UCB1, and its regret must bend over on the easy bandit.
hints: Each draw is independent. Do not share one sample between arms, and do not draw more than once per arm per pull.
losses = counts[i] - totals[i] is a float because rewards are floats; betavariate accepts it.
The scripted generator in the check raises an error if you call rng.random(): Thompson sampling needs nothing but betavariate.
milestones.solution:
def thompson(counts, totals, t, rng):
    """Draw one sample from Beta(1 + wins, 1 + losses) for each arm and pull the arm with the largest draw.
    Draw the arms in index order, one rng.betavariate call each."""
    best, best_draw = 0, -1.0
    for i, (n, s) in enumerate(zip(counts, totals)):
        draw = rng.betavariate(1.0 + s, 1.0 + (n - s))
        if draw > best_draw:
            best, best_draw = i, draw
    return best
milestones.explain:
UCB1 turns uncertainty into a bonus you add. Thompson sampling (Thompson, 1933) turns it into randomness. Keep a belief about each arm's win rate, draw one sample from each belief, and pull the arm whose sample is largest. For an arm with w wins and l losses, a natural belief is the Beta distribution with parameters (1 + w, 1 + l): it starts as a flat distribution over [0, 1] for an untried arm, gets a peak at the observed win rate, and narrows as evidence accumulates. Python draws from it with rng.betavariate(alpha, beta). Here is what these beliefs look like in numbers:

import random, statistics
from solution import *

rng = random.Random(0)
print("what a belief looks like: 20,000 draws from Beta(1 + wins, 1 + losses)")
for wins, losses in ((0, 0), (3, 1), (7, 3), (70, 30)):
    draws = [rng.betavariate(1 + wins, 1 + losses) for _ in range(20_000)]
    print(f"  {wins:>2} wins, {losses:>2} losses: mean {statistics.mean(draws):.3f}  spread (sd) {statistics.pstdev(draws):.3f}")
$ python3 exp_beta.py
what a belief looks like: 20,000 draws from Beta(1 + wins, 1 + losses)
   0 wins,  0 losses: mean 0.500  spread (sd) 0.289
   3 wins,  1 losses: mean 0.667  spread (sd) 0.179
   7 wins,  3 losses: mean 0.667  spread (sd) 0.132
  70 wins, 30 losses: mean 0.696  spread (sd) 0.045

The belief after 7 wins and 3 losses has the same mean as the belief after 3 wins and 1 loss (0.667) but is narrower, and 100 pulls pin the win rate down to within about 0.045. Arms we know little about have wide beliefs, so they occasionally produce a high draw and get pulled; arms we know well produce draws close to their mean. Exploration emerges from the spread, and fades as the spread does, with no constant to tune. That is much of why Thompson sampling is popular in production recommenders.

When you run the check, it first uses a scripted random generator to confirm the Beta parameters you pass (1 + wins, 1 + losses) and the order of the calls, then runs the experiment. After that the league table below is printed from your own code: five policies on three problems, mean regret after 2,000 pulls. Find where each policy wins and where it loses.
milestones.card:
One way to explore is to keep a belief about each arm's win rate, draw one random sample from each belief, and pull the arm whose sample is largest (Thompson sampling). An arm you know little about has a wide belief, so it sometimes draws high and gets pulled. As evidence arrives the belief narrows and the exploring fades by itself, with no constant to tune.

The belief for an arm with w wins and l losses is a Beta distribution: a curve over win rates from 0 to 1. The 1 + in the parameters makes it flat when nothing is known. Wins are totals[i]; losses are the pulls that did not win. rng.betavariate(a, b) draws one sample, and the draw order matters, so go through the arms in index order. Return the arm with the largest draw. Untried arms need no special case.

0 wins, 0 losses: flat, mean 0.500, standard deviation 0.289
70 wins, 30 losses: mean 0.696, standard deviation 0.045

milestones.title: the four phases of MCTS
milestones.task: Write uct_value(wins, visits, parent_visits, c), select_child(node, c) (highest UCT value among the children; ties to the first), expand(node, game, rng) (take one random untried move out of node.untried, create and attach the child, return it) and backpropagate(node, result).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand values for uct_value (2 wins in 3 visits under a parent with 4 visits at c = 1 is 2/3 + √(ln 4 / 3) = 1.35, the number from the chapter's stepper); select_child on a two-child tree under three constants (1: the well-won child; 3: the barely visited one; 0: the win rate decides); nine expansions of the empty tic-tac-toe board that must produce nine distinct, correctly linked children; and the exact chain of the figure above, including a draw.
hints: uct_value is the formula in one line. Use math.log (natural log) and take the square root of the whole ratio.
select_child never sees an unvisited child: every child was created by expand and then visited once in the same iteration. So visits >= 1 and there is no division by zero.

expand: node.untried.pop(rng.randrange(len(node.untried))) removes the move. Then Node(game, game.next(node.state, move), parent=node, move=move) and append it to node.children. Forgetting to remove the move is the classic bug: the same position is expanded again and again.
backpropagate is a loop: add to visits and wins, set result = 1.0 - result, step to node.parent, stop at None. If your check says the wins are all 1.0, you forgot the flip.
milestones.solution:
def uct_value(wins, visits, parent_visits, c):
    """wins/visits + c * sqrt(ln(parent_visits) / visits)."""
    return wins / visits + c * math.sqrt(math.log(parent_visits) / visits)

def select_child(node, c):
    """The child with the highest UCT value (ties to the first in the list). All children must have visits >= 1."""
    best, best_value = None, -math.inf
    for child in node.children:
        v = uct_value(child.wins, child.visits, node.visits, c)
        if v > best_value:
            best, best_value = child, v
    return best

def expand(node, game, rng):
    """Remove one random untried move from the node, add the child for it, and return the child."""
    move = node.untried.pop(rng.randrange(len(node.untried)))
    child = Node(game, game.next(node.state, move), parent=node, move=move)
    node.children.append(child)
    return child

def backpropagate(node, result):
    """`result` is the reward for the player who moved into `node`. Add a visit and the reward to the node and
    every ancestor, flipping the result (1 - result) at every level."""
    while node is not None:
        node.visits += 1
        node.wins += result
        result = 1.0 - result
        node = node.parent
milestones.explain:
A bandit has one decision. A game has a sequence of them, each opening a new set of choices. Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) treats every position in the game as its own small bandit, whose arms are the legal moves and whose reward is eventually winning. Kocsis and Szepesvári (2006) applied UCB1 to trees and called the result UCT. The tree is grown one iteration at a time, and each iteration has four phases:

  1. Selection. From the root, walk down the tree. At each node whose moves have all been tried, go to the child with the highest UCT value.
  2. Expansion. At a node that still has an untried move, add one child for it.
  3. Simulation (a rollout). From the new node, play random moves to the end of the game and note who won. (Given.)
  4. Backpropagation. Walk back up the path, adding one visit and the result to every node.

The UCT value of a child is the UCB1 formula with the win rate in place of the average and the parent's visit count in place of t: wins/visits + c √(ln parent_visits / visits).

The one subtle thing is perspective. In a two-player game a result that is good for me is bad for you. The code stores, in each node, wins for the player who moved into that node. A node's parent is the position where the other player chooses among its children, so the parent wants the child with the best wins / visits from the mover's point of view, which is exactly what the node holds. The price is that backpropagation must flip the result at every level:

Draws count as 0.5 for both sides, and 1 − 0.5 = 0.5, so the same flip works. The given rollout function already returns its result in this convention (the reward for the player who moved into the state it was given), and game.terminal_value(state) is defined the same way, so you never need to ask whose turn it is. A Node holds its state, parent, move, children, the list of moves not yet expanded (untried), visits and wins.
milestones.card:
Tree search treats every position in a game as a small bandit (a choice among slot machines): the arms are the legal moves, and the payout is eventually winning. The tree grows one iteration at a time: select a path down by UCB1, expand it with one new child, play a random game from that child (the rollout, already written), and backpropagate the result up the path.

uct_value(wins, visits, parent_visits, c) is UCB1 for one child: its win rate plus an exploration bonus, with the parent's visits in place of t. select_child takes the highest value. expand picks a random move from node.untried, removes it, attaches a new Node for it as a child and returns it. backpropagate adds one visit to the node and every ancestor. A node's wins count for the player who moved into it, so the result flips to 1 - result at each step up.

uct_value(2, 3, 4, 1) = 2/3 + sqrt(ln 4 / 3) = 1.35
a rollout won by the leaf's mover adds to wins from the leaf up: 1, 0, 1, 0

Read more: A7 chapter 1, from one decision to a tree.

milestones.title: the search loop, tested on Nim
milestones.task: Write mcts(game, state, iters, rng, c=1.0, rollout_fn=rollout) (return the root) and best_move(root) (the move of the most-visited child; ties to the first).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Tiny games with known answers (pile 1: one move, always won; pile 2: take both); the bookkeeping invariants above on 500-iteration searches from a pile of 12; determinism; a finished game; then pile 10 with 2,000 iterations, where at least 90% of the visits must go to taking 2 and it must have the best win rate; and a table of how often the most-visited move is a winning one on piles 1 to 12 at 10, 200 and 1,000 iterations (at least 85% at 200 and 95% at 1,000).
hints: Selection: while not node.untried and node.children: node = select_child(node, c). Then if node.untried: node = expand(node, game, rng). Then result = rollout_fn(game, node.state, rng) and backpropagate(node, result).

The result passed to backpropagate is already in the right convention: rollout returns the reward for the player who moved into the state you gave it, and node.state is the state that player moved into.
If visits are lopsided in the wrong direction, check that select_child compares children from the parent's perspective (it does, as long as wins is stored for the mover into the child).
best_move: max(root.children, key=lambda ch: ch.visits).move returns the first of equals.
milestones.solution:
def mcts(game, state, iters, rng, c=1.0, rollout_fn=rollout):
    """Run `iters` iterations of selection, expansion, simulation and backpropagation from `state`.
    Returns the root node."""
    root = Node(game, state)
    for _ in range(iters):
        node = root
        # 1. selection: descend while the node is fully expanded and has children
        while not node.untried and node.children:
            node = select_child(node, c)
        # 2. expansion: add one new child (a terminal node has nothing to expand)
        if node.untried:
            node = expand(node, game, rng)
        # 3. simulation: score the new position by playing it out
        result = rollout_fn(game, node.state, rng)
        # 4. backpropagation
        backpropagate(node, result)
    return root

def best_move(root):
    """The move of the most-visited child (not the highest win rate). Ties go to the first child."""
    best = max(root.children, key=lambda ch: ch.visits)
    return best.move
milestones.explain:
Now assemble the iteration. mcts(game, state, iters, rng, c, rollout_fn) creates a root node and repeats the four phases iters times. Selection descends while a node has no untried moves and does have children (a node with nothing untried and no children is a finished game: stay there). Expansion happens only if the node has an untried move. The rollout function is a parameter, so milestone 6 can swap it. The root is returned, and the tree it holds is the result: the visit counts at the root's children are the search's opinion of the moves.

What to play with that opinion is the other function, best_move(root). The tempting choice is the child with the highest win rate. The right one is the child with the most visits. A child with a 100% win rate from one lucky visit has been barely examined, while a child with 1,940 visits and a 95% win rate has survived thousands of attempts to refute it; and because selection steers visits towards the moves that keep looking best, the visit count is a robust summary of the whole search. Here is the tree your code should build from a pile of 10 stones after 2,000 iterations (real output of exp_tree.py below):

import random
from solution import *

root = mcts(Nim(), 10, 2000, random.Random(0))
print(f"root: pile {root.state}, {root.visits} visits")
for k in sorted(root.children, key=lambda k: k.move):
    print(f"  take {k.move} -> pile {k.state}: visits {k.visits:>4d}, wins {k.wins:7.1f}, win rate {k.wins / k.visits:.2f}")
best = max(root.children, key=lambda k: k.visits)
print(f"best child's children (pile {best.state}):")
for k in sorted(best.children, key=lambda k: k.move):
    print(f"  take {k.move} -> pile {k.state}: visits {k.visits:>4d}, wins {k.wins:7.1f}, win rate {k.wins / k.visits:.2f}")
$ python3 exp_tree.py
root: pile 10, 2000 visits
  take 1 -> pile 9: visits   22, wins     7.0, win rate 0.32
  take 2 -> pile 8: visits 1940, wins  1842.0, win rate 0.95
  take 3 -> pile 7: visits   38, wins    17.0, win rate 0.45
best child's children (pile 8):
  take 1 -> pile 7: visits  669, wins    35.0, win rate 0.05
  take 2 -> pile 6: visits  649, wins    33.0, win rate 0.05
  take 3 -> pile 5: visits  621, wins    30.0, win rate 0.05

Nim is a good test because it has a known answer: leave your opponent a multiple of 4 and you win, so from 10 the right move is to take 2. Nothing in mcts knows that rule; it learns it from simulated games. The check also tests the bookkeeping that tree-search bugs break. The root's visits must equal the iterations. Every non-root node with children must have visits equal to one (the iteration that created it) plus its children's visits. A rollout function that always returns 0.5 must leave every node with wins equal to half its visits, which fails immediately if the flip in backpropagation is wrong. And searching from a finished game must not crash.
milestones.card:
Tree search repeats one iteration (select a path, expand one child, simulate a random game, backpropagate the result) many times and keeps the tree it grows. Selection sends more visits to moves that keep looking good, so the visit counts at the root's children become the search's opinion of each move.

mcts creates a root Node. Then, iters times, it walks down with select_child while the current node has no untried moves but does have children, calls expand only if the node has an untried move, scores the node with rollout_fn and hands the result to backpropagate. A node with neither untried moves nor children is a finished game: stay on it. Return the root. best_move returns the move of the child with the most visits, not the highest win rate: one lucky visit gives a perfect win rate, but many visits mean the move survived many attempts to refute it.

milestones.task: Write smart_rollout(game, state, rng) and mcts_player(game, iters, c=1.0, rollout_fn=rollout), which returns a function player(state, rng) that runs mcts and plays best_move.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. By hand: from XX.OO.... X (to move) wins at once, so the reward for O, who moved into that state, must be exactly 0.0 on every seed; finished games return their final value; rollouts from the empty board draw much more often than random play does. Then tactics: in four must-block positions the player with smart_rollout and only 30 iterations must find the one saving move in at least 80% of 60 seeds, and more often than the player with random rollouts. Finally full games: 600 iterations never lose to a random player and win at least 80% of 40 games, and 1,500 iterations draw (or at worst lose one of) 40 games against the perfect player, but 30 iterations are visibly easier to beat.
hints: mcts_player is four lines: define player(state, rng), call mcts(game, state, iters, rng, c, rollout_fn), return best_move(root), and return player.

smart_rollout starts as a copy of rollout. Inside the loop, loop over game.legal(state): for each move look at nxt = game.next(state, m). If nxt is terminal and game.terminal_value(nxt) == 1.0 the move wins immediately. Otherwise it is safe if no reply r in game.legal(nxt) gives a terminal state with value 1.0.
Do not forget the flip bookkeeping from the given rollout: count how many moves were played and convert the final value at the end.
If the block test fails only for the smart player, test smart_rollout directly on the positions of the check: from XX.OO.... it must always return 0.0.
milestones.solution:
def smart_rollout(game, state, rng):
    """A rollout that is random except for two cheap rules, applied at every ply:
    1. if some legal move wins the game on the spot, play it;
    2. otherwise avoid any move that lets the opponent win on the spot, if such a safe move exists.
    Returns the reward for the player who moved INTO `state`, exactly like `rollout`."""
    flipped = False
    while not game.is_terminal(state):
        moves = game.legal(state)
        choice = None
        safe = []
        for m in moves:
            nxt = game.next(state, m)
            if game.is_terminal(nxt) and game.terminal_value(nxt) == 1.0:
                choice = m
                break
            if not any(game.is_terminal(game.next(nxt, r)) and game.terminal_value(game.next(nxt, r)) == 1.0
                       for r in game.legal(nxt)):
                safe.append(m)
        if choice is None:
            choice = rng.choice(safe or moves)
        state = game.next(state, choice)
        flipped = not flipped
    value = game.terminal_value(state)
    return 1.0 - value if flipped else value

def mcts_player(game, iters, c=1.0, rollout_fn=rollout):
    """A player function `player(state, rng) -> move` that runs MCTS for `iters` iterations and plays the most-visited move."""
    def player(state, rng):
        return best_move(mcts(game, state, iters, rng, c, rollout_fn))
    return player
milestones.explain:
Tic-tac-toe has a known value (a draw with perfect play), a state space small enough for an exact solver, and enough tactics to expose a weak searcher. The starter gives you the game, a random_player, a minimax_player that plays perfectly (it memoises the exact value of every position), and play_game(game, first, second, rng). A player is a function player(state, rng) -> move. You write the player that wraps your search, and a smarter rollout.

The position on the left is the kind of thing a search with few iterations gets wrong. X threatens to complete the top row at cell 2, and O has only one move that avoids losing: take cell 2. Under random rollouts, a bad move such as cell 6 still wins a fair share of the random games that follow, because X, playing randomly, usually fails to see its own winning move. The search needs many iterations before the refutation dominates. A rollout with two cheap rules is much sharper:

  1. If some legal move wins the game on the spot, play it.
  2. Otherwise avoid any move after which the opponent can win on the spot, if a safe move exists. (Choose uniformly among the safe moves; if none is safe, among all.)

Everything else stays random. The rules use only the game interface (legal, next, is_terminal, terminal_value), so they work for any two-player game of this shape. It is the pre-neural-network fix mentioned in chapter 1: put a little domain knowledge in the rollout policy. Remember that smart_rollout must return its result in the same convention as rollout, the reward for the player who moved into the state it was given.
milestones.card:
A random rollout (a random game played to the end to score a position) is a weak judge. A blunder can still look good, because the opponent, also playing randomly, often misses its own winning move. A rollout that grabs a win when it can, and otherwise avoids handing the opponent one, sees the danger at once, so the search needs far fewer iterations.

smart_rollout is the given rollout with a better move choice at every ply (each move by either player). A move wins on the spot if, after game.next, the state is terminal and game.terminal_value is 1.0 (a draw is 0.5). A move is safe if no legal reply from the new state wins on the spot. Use only the game interface, so any game works, and copy rollout's bookkeeping for whose reward is returned. mcts_player(game, iters, c, rollout_fn) returns a function player(state, rng) that runs mcts and plays best_move.
